red.focus: From royal command to public law
red.summary: Begin with Hammurabi's Babylon to see why rulers put legal decisions in public form. Learn what an inscribed judgment could accomplish—and what it could not guarantee.
checklist: I can identify Hammurabi's monument and its purpose
I can explain the difference between a public rule and equal protection
I can connect visible legal rules to claims of royal authority

sections.title: The King Makes Justice Visible
sections.body_md: Around 1750 BCE, King Hammurabi of Babylon presented a large inscribed monument recording judgments about property, family, commerce and injury. Its carved scene associated royal authority with the sun god Shamash. The monument did not operate like a complete modern statute book: it offered a collection of legal judgments and examples. Its significance is that a ruler publicly represented the administration of justice as a duty of kingship, not just an occasional personal order.
sections.audio_script: Around 1750 BCE, King Hammurabi of Babylon presented a large inscribed monument recording judgments about property, family, commerce and injury. Its carved scene associated royal authority with the sun god Shamash. The monument did not operate like a complete modern statute book: it offered a collection of legal judgments and examples. Its significance is that a ruler publicly represented the administration of justice as a duty of kingship, not just an occasional personal order.

sections.title: An Inscription Is a Claim
sections.body_md: Putting judgments in stone made legal expectations visible and more durable than an unrecorded royal command. A reader could see that a dispute about payment or bodily injury was treated as part of an organized legal order. But the monument's public existence does not prove that everyone could read it, invoke it equally, or obtain a fair hearing. Historical evidence requires us to distinguish what a ruler claimed about justice from how officials actually treated people.

sections.title: The First Historical Question
sections.body_md: Compare a robber demanding money with a king demanding a lawful tax. The difference cannot be understood only by the power to punish; it includes a claim of authority, an announced norm and institutions to apply it. Hammurabi's monument makes that claim especially visible. Yet a legal historian must ask whose consent mattered, what groups received protection, and who could challenge a decision. Public law can both restrain violence and legitimize unequal power.

yellow.focus: Roman legal authority and its changing institutions
yellow.summary: Move from Babylonian kingship to Roman republican and imperial lawmaking. Distinguish legislation, magistrates, jurists and imperial enactments instead of treating Roman law as a single voice.
checklist: I can distinguish the Twelve Tables from imperial legislation
I can identify the role of Roman jurists and magistrates
I can explain why Roman legal authority changed over time

sections.title: The Twelve Tables
sections.body_md: In the mid-fifth century BCE, Rome produced the Twelve Tables, traditionally associated with publicizing rules after conflict over access to legal knowledge. The original tablets have not survived, and later writers transmit fragments of their content. The episode matters because it linked legitimate legal authority with publicly knowable standards rather than exclusive control of custom by a narrow group. It did not create modern equality or end Roman hierarchy. Its value is historical and institutional, not mythical.
sections.audio_script: In the mid-fifth century BCE, Rome produced the Twelve Tables, traditionally associated with publicizing rules after conflict over access to legal knowledge. sections.title: More Than One Lawmaker
sections.body_md: Roman law developed through statutes, magistrates' edicts, juristic interpretation and eventually imperial constitutions. Praetors shaped available legal actions, while trained jurists reasoned about disputes and legal categories. During the empire, the emperor's enactments gained substantial importance. Describing all of this as 'Roman law' can obscure changes in who could produce an authoritative norm. To understand a rule, ask its period, source, intended audience and method of application before attributing it to an emperor or senate.

sections.title: Authority as a Legal Argument
sections.body_md: Consider a dispute in imperial Rome. A lawyer might draw on an enacted rule, an established procedural form or respected juristic interpretation, but the weight of each source varied by era. The existence of multiple legal sources required methods for reconciling them. That is the bridge to modern research: identifying a rule means identifying the institution or practice giving it force. The legal historian should resist reading today's neat hierarchy of sources backward into every Roman century.

orange.focus: Competing medieval authorities and the rise of constraint
orange.summary: Study medieval legal pluralism and the negotiated limits imposed on rulers. Explain why a royal charter's significance must be read against feudal privilege and competing jurisdictions.
checklist: I can compare royal, ecclesiastical and local jurisdictions
I can explain the historical limits of Magna Carta
I can analyze how a written charter could constrain monarchy

sections.title: Law Without One Exclusive Center
sections.body_md: Medieval European communities could encounter royal courts, local customs, feudal jurisdictions and ecclesiastical law. Each institution claimed authority in particular matters, sometimes with overlapping boundaries. A marriage question and a land dispute might travel through different legal routes. This was not simply confusion awaiting modern central government; legal pluralism reflected competing institutions and social relationships. Understanding it prevents the mistaken assumption that a modern national court hierarchy is law's natural starting point.

sections.title: Magna Carta in Its Own Time
sections.body_md: Magna Carta emerged from a crisis between King John and rebel barons in 1215. It protected specified liberties and imposed commitments on royal action, especially toward free people within the charter's political order. It was not a modern universal bill of rights. Its later constitutional significance developed through reissues, reinterpretation and political struggle. An expert separates the text's immediate bargaining context from the broader principle later readers drew from it: even royal power can be held to lawful forms.

sections.title: Constraining the Source of Law
sections.body_md: A charter creates an especially difficult authority question. If a king issues or accepts a limitation on his power, why must later officials honor it when inconvenient? The answer may involve oath, custom, recognition by institutions and the costs of breach. Magna Carta's influence cannot be measured solely by its immediate compliance. Its historical importance also lies in how later generations invoked it to challenge arbitrary action. The historian must track each reinterpretation rather than assume one unbroken meaning.

black.focus: Codification, source hierarchy and the legitimacy of legal order
black.summary: Examine Justinian's compilation and later codification as projects that select what counts as authoritative law. Evaluate how organizing inherited materials can both clarify legal obligations and concentrate political power.
checklist: I can distinguish compilation from the creation of entirely new law
I can evaluate codification as an assertion of institutional authority
I can criticize a source hierarchy that hides excluded traditions

sections.title: Justinian's Legal Project
sections.body_md: Under Emperor Justinian I in the sixth century, scholars compiled and reorganized Roman legal materials, including juristic writings and imperial enactments, in works later known collectively as the Corpus Juris Civilis. The project was not merely a neutral library catalog. Selection and official promulgation were ways to establish which texts could claim current authority. Much inherited reasoning was preserved through imperial control over its presentation. Codification can therefore preserve legal knowledge while reshaping its institutional meaning.
sections.audio_script: Under Emperor Justinian I in the sixth century, scholars compiled and reorganized Roman legal materials, including juristic writings and imperial enactments, in works later known collectively as the Corpus Juris Civilis. The project was not merely a neutral library catalog. Selection and official promulgation were ways to establish which texts could claim current authority. Much inherited reasoning was preserved through imperial control over its presentation. Codification can therefore preserve legal knowledge while reshaping its institutional meaning.

sections.title: The Promise and Price of a Code
sections.body_md: A code offers accessibility, system and a relatively visible hierarchy among sources. Yet the apparent completeness of a written code may suppress local practice, minority norms or interpretive disagreement. The Napoleonic Civil Code of 1804 illustrates the later ambition to organize private law into general legislative rules, while practical legal reasoning still depended on interpretation. The doctoral question is not whether codes are good or bad; it is what authority they claim, what they simplify and whose lived legal world they leave out.

sections.title: Authority After Conquest and Reform
sections.body_md: A state may declare that an imported code replaces earlier customs, but formal enactment does not by itself settle whether people experience the system as legitimate. Colonial administration and postcolonial reform make this distinction especially sharp. Analyze source hierarchy, access to adjudication, recognition of local traditions and the opportunity of affected communities to contest the rule. A legally valid enactment can be a powerful fact, while a legitimate legal order requires a deeper justification rooted in accountability and the people subject to it.
